analysis.one_liner: Makes offshore oil companies pay all costs of their spills, removing the $75 million cap.
analysis.headline: The bill to lift the $75 million offshore oil spill liability cap was introduced with 16 Senate Democrats and died in committee without a vote when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Oil Pollution Act of 1990, a company responsible for an offshore oil spill must pay all cleanup costs, but its liability for other damages — ruined fisheries, lost tourism revenue, harm to natural resources, extra public services — is capped at $75 million. This bill would delete that cap and make the polluter liable for all covered damages. It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never moved before Congress adjourned.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities, fishing and tourism businesses, state and local governments, and taxpayers. When a spill's damage exceeds $75 million, today the excess costs fall on victims and public budgets; this bill would put those costs back on the company that caused the spill.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal residents, fishing towns, and taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: Removes the $75 million cap on an offshore spiller's liability beyond cleanup costs, so victims of a major spill could recover their actual losses ([S2], [S3]).
Adds explicit coverage for damages to natural resources, property, revenue, and profits, plus the cost of extra public services like fire protection during spill response ([S2]).

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas companies, which would face unlimited financial exposure for spills — costs they would have to carry through insurance, reserves, or higher prices.

drawbacks.text: Unlimited liability raises the cost and risk of offshore drilling, which the industry argues could be absorbed mainly by large companies able to self-insure, squeezing out smaller operators ([S3]).

Higher expected spill costs could be passed through to consumers in fuel prices, and some economists argue unlimited liability does not proportionally improve spill prevention once a firm cannot bear the worst-case loss.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is straightforward: it shifts catastrophic spill costs from victims and taxpayers to the companies profiting from offshore drilling. The main cost is higher drilling insurance and compliance expenses, some of which could reach consumers at the pump. The bill contains no special-interest carve-outs; its text is a two-line amendment striking the cap.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final weeks of the 115th Congress and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Menendez introduced the bill on December 13, 2018, and it was read twice and referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee ([S1], [S5]).
That was its last action: no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed, and the bill expired when the 115th Congress ended ([S5]).
All 15 cosponsors were Democrats, joining Menendez; no Republican signed on ([S4]).

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil companies keep the $75 million liability cap, leaving damage above that limit with spill victims, coastal communities, and public budgets.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore oil drillers keep the liability cap

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to remove the $75 million offshore spill liability cap and referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee.

for.name: 15 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Markey, Reed, Booker, Blumenthal, Whitehouse, Peters, Klobuchar, Merkley, Shaheen, Durbin, Gillibrand, Harris, Feinstein, Smith, Hassan)

against.name: Sen. John Barrasso
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or hearing before the Congress expired.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 sponsors and cosponsors were Senate Democrats, and the Republican-chaired committee took no action on the bill ([S4]).

industries.note: The bill removes their $75 million cap on spill liability, exposing them to unlimited damages for disasters like Deepwater Horizon. Their interest in keeping the cap runs against coastal residents and taxpayers who absorb spill costs above the limit.

industries.industry: Offshore insurers and energy financial markets
industries.note: Unlimited liability would raise premiums and reserve requirements for covering offshore operations; some of that cost could pass to consumers, while spill victims would gain a larger pool to claim against.
